themes.theme_description: What is Geography? Ways of studying Geography. Physical Environment.

topics.core_competency: After studying this topic, the learner should be able to understand and appreciate the importance of studying geography.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: use fieldwork to observe, name and classify human and physical features (s, gs)
know the meaning of geography and environment (k)
understand that the environment is all the things around us (u)
realise that geography is a study of the relationship between people and their environment, both natural and man made (u)
appreciate that the study of geography helps us to understand how our lives are affected by the environment, and how we can preserve the environment so it remains useful to us (a, gs)
appreciate that caring for and preserving resources in the local environment, community and country are signs of love for one’s country

suggested_learning_activities.description: In groups, learners: Explore and identify 'natural' and 'built' features of the local environment by annotating photographs or labelling the environment through fieldwork sketches; discuss before agreeing the definition of these terms and making final adjustments; investigate, name and categorise features on photographs in different environments.
As a whole class, learners contribute to a collaborative display of feature names, classifying them as 'natural' or 'built'.
Learners: use a range of media: case studies, books, visitor- talks and Internet research, as well as their own work, to debate and agree what geography means.
discuss the importance of studying geography, using examples from things they do every day, such as collecting water and deciding on when to plant or harvest certain crops.

discuss, identify and list ways that they and their family use the local environment; they identify how other people and animals use places in different ways. They debate the question 'Whose environment is it?' and jointly compile a action plan or charter for environmental care for their local area.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe learners as they discuss and amend their work; ask learners to explain their categorisation of natural and built features.
In conversation, ask learners to explain how people in the school are affected by the physical environment; and give an example of how people have changed the physical environment.
Assess the learners’ manifesto.

topic_metadata.topic_title: SHOWING THE LOCAL AREA ON A MAP

topics.core_competency: After studying this topic, the learner should know the main physical and human features of the local area and how these can be shown on a map.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: know what a map is and how this can be used to show places. (k)
understand the difference between a map and a photograph (u, s)
understand that maps are representations of the world at different scales (u)
be able to draw a sketch map of the school and/or the local area (s)
be able to use and interpret symbols and identify features on a map using a key (s)
be able to identify directions on a map using basic compass points (s)
be able to follow routes on a map (s)
be able to use the local area maps drawn in (c) above to find information about people living in the local area (s)

suggested_learning_activities.description: Learners use globes, a range of maps (including digital maps) and aerial images to investigate what a map is and what it might show.
Learners draw a map to show a visitor to the area how to get to the school (do not tell them how to draw it). They compare and evaluate each other’s maps and identify ways to improve them.
Through fieldwork, learners use maps and compasses to orient themselves and sketch what they can see in that direction, annotating features.
In pairs, learners draw a map to show the route from their school to home, indicating physical and human features using a key, and then swap maps so they can find out where the other person lives.
Learners use their own and other maps to help them ask and answer questions about their local area.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe learners explaining what a map is and examine their written definitions.
Learners use their own maps to explain what the local area is like.
Learners discuss the qualities of a good map and evaluate each other’s. Observe what they produce to describe their findings.
In conversation, evaluate how well learners answer questions using given maps about the relationship between maps and photographs.

topics.core_competency: After studying this topic, the learner should know the main features of a map and understand the differences between a map and reality.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: draw a sketch map of the school and/or the local area
use and interpret symbols and identify features on a map using a key (s)
identify directions on a map, using basic compass points (s)
follow routes on a map (s)
draw a map using a simple scale and use scale on a map (s)
use letter and number co-ordinates or bearings and directions to locate places on a map (s)
locate places on an atlas map using latitude and longitude and describe the places from information on the map (s)
understand the difference between a map and a photograph (u, s)
understand that there are many types of maps on different scales (u)
use a linear scale and representative fraction to estinate distance, area and size of features on a map(s)

suggested_learning_activities.description: Show a photograph of a person and ask learners to compare this with the real size of the person or, if they have a mobile phone, take a 'selfie' and ask them if it is their real size.

Explain: All things on a photograph or map reduce items or objects by the same amount so, to get the real size, you multiply e.g. 1 cm. on photograph = 10 cms. in real size. This is called a representative fraction i.e. 1:10
Learners are challenged to produce a sketch map of an area showing comparative size, shape and distance. They calculate representative fractions to help them do this.
Learners use paper and digital maps at different scales to measure and compare distances between features of their locality e.g. their home and school, nearest town, river etc.

Learners measure areas, distance and length of features on maps to ask and answer questions about a locale e.g. about patterns of land use. They investigate types of symbols used on a map and devise some of their own.
Learners play games using grid references to find hidden objects out of doors or use these as clues to guess the feature on a map.
Learners use globe-tossing activities to find places, using latitude and longitude clues and then they write their own clues.
Activity to locate places using a grid.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe learners as they discuss and problem-solve how to make a scaled map.
Observe how well learners explain what their maps show, using language of scale.
Learners use survey maps, as well as their own maps, to ask and answer questions about places at different scales. In conversation, ask learners to explain their views.
Observe how well learners explain what their maps show about patterns and type of land use, with reference to size, scale and the key.

syllabus_notes.text_verbatim: Explain that maps show real directions.
Explain compass bearings based on degrees of circle.

topic_metadata.topic_title: WAYS OF STUDYING GEOGRAPHY: FIELD WORK, PHOTOGRAPHS, STATISTICS, CHARTS AND GRAPHS

time_allocation.unit: periods plus time outside the classroom

topics.core_competency: After studying this topic, the learner should understand and be able to study geography through the use of field work and through studying photographs.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: know what is meant by field work (k)
understand how to use and apply different techniques used in field work (u)
use observation, interviews, questionnaires, drawings and photographs in field work (s)
use maps, aerial images, photographs, graphs and charts to communicate data (s)
analyse and present statistics gathered in fieldwork (s);
write conclusions to summarise field work (gs)
know the three different angles from which photographs can be taken (k)
know the terms used to describe the different parts of a photograph (k)
appreciate the effect of perspective on oblique photographs (v, a)
differentiate between photographs and maps (u)
describe an area seen on a photograph (s)
make a sketch of an area from a photograph (s)
appreciate that field work and photographs are important because geography is the study of the real world (v, a, gs)
use field work to study a trading centre, town or other urban area or any other area (s, u)

must_cover: Techniques: observation, interviews, questionnaires, drawings, photographs
Photo types: Ground, oblique, vertical aerial
Photo terminology: foreground, middle ground, background

suggested_learning_activities.description: Discuss ways of finding about people and places. Learners should consider these ways of studying geography and begin to evaluate their effectiveness: using media; reading research; interpreting maps; analysing data and charts etc; interpreting reports; field study.

Challenge learners, individually or in groups to suggest their own topic, objectives and methods to collect information about the local area. They should conduct a field study, compare findings and share opinions about different methods of data collection. (Interviews, questionnaires, measurement, sketches, data analysis.)

Show photographs taken from the ground, a high angle and the air. Ask what the differences are. Explain that photographs can be taken from different angles: from the ground, from the air but looking at an angle (oblique aerial), from the air looking vertically down (vertical aerial)

Explain that it is useful to draw a sketch to show the area on a photograph. Learners practise this: Draw a frame the same size as the photo. Divide it into 3 or 4 areas which are similar e.g. forest, houses, banana crop, road, lake etc. and shade or colour and label these.
Explain that many photographs of areas they will study are available on the Internet. Give learners a topic or area to find relevant photographs on the Internet

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe learners planning their enquiry, the results achieved and their evaluation of the process.
Observe how learners present findings; they should explain how they have carried out an enquiry through fieldwork and what aspects were particularly useful.

syllabus_notes.text_verbatim: Note north is not necessarily at the top in photographs, so do not use north etc.

topics.core_competency: After studying this topic, the learner should understand the relationship between the Earth and the sun and the effects this has on our lives.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: understand the relationship between the Earth and the sun and how this affects temperatures and seasons (u)

draw diagrams to show the relationship between the Earth and the sun’s rays and the causes of temperature variations and use these to show why the Earth can be divided into tropical, temperate and polar regions (s)
understand how the rotation causes day and night (u)
know how we can locate places on a globe by using a grid including the use of latitude and longitude. (u)
use and measure latitude and longitude (s)
calculate time using longitude (s)
appreciate how the movement of the Earth in relation to the Sun affects the way people live: the effect of temperatures and seasons, lengths of day and night (a, gs)

must_cover: Special lines: Equator, Tropics, Arctic/Antarctic circles

suggested_learning_activities.description: Learners are given a set of 'True' and 'False' statements about the rotation of the Earth and its orbit around the sun and carry out research in groups to identify the correct answers. They use their chosen facts to illustrate a demonstration of the Earth in motion over a twenty-for hour and yearly cycle, using models and spoken explanation.

Learners work in groups to: investigate, using a globe or football and light source, how the energy from the sun reaches different parts of the Earth when it is tilted on its axis and in orbit around the sun

Individually, learners draw their own diagrams and label them, writing a short explanation of how temperature variation occurs over the Earth throughout the year and how this causes different climatic zones.
Learners play globe-tossing games using a blow -up globe and respond to questions about latitude and longitude with increasing difficulty, developing their own questions to ask each other.
Learners investigate webcams in different cities, East and West of where they are, to compare time zones and describe what is happening there; they use a map of world time zones to help them do this.
Learners do some exercises to find time in different places.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe learners as they demonstrate their models and give a spoken explanation of the processes at work.
Observe learners’ models and drawn diagrams, and their spoken and written explanations with appropriate vocabulary.
In conversation, ask learners to explain how longitude and latitude are used to locate places on Earth.
Learners explain how longitude is used to calculate time and produce written calculations of time difference.
Learners identify a place in another climate zone, explain how daily life might differ and explain why.

syllabus_notes.text_verbatim: Look on the Internet to find maps of world time zones.

topics.core_competency: After studying this topic, the learner should know and understand the main elements of the weather, their causes and how to measure them.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: understand the differences between weather and climate (u)
understand the elements of weather and how they are measured (u)
carry out a project to observe, measure and record the elements of weather, make suitable instruments and visit a weather station(s)
know the names of the main instruments used for recording the different elements of the weather and how each one is used (k)
know what a Stevenson screen looks like, how it is built and why it is used (k)
know the terms used for plotting weather on maps (k)
know the names and characteristics of the main kinds of clouds and rainfall. (k)
appreciate that people’s lifestyles are influenced by the type of weather and climate (a)
understand the positive and negative effects of the weather on their own lives and those of their communities (u)
be able to draw climate graphs of local and other areas and describe climates using these (s)

practicals.title: Weather Station Visit / Instrument Making
practicals.description_verbatim: Learners visit a working weather station to research the components of a weather station and how they work. They name, describe and practise using the tools and approaches they have seen and make their own equipment, where practical, such as Okta grids for measuring cloud cover and rain gauges.

practicals.title: Weather Diary
practicals.description_verbatim: Group learners and guide them to start a weather diary to record daily weather, either by instruments, if available, or by observation e.g. dry, wet, very wet; sunny, cloudy; hot, warm, cold; wind strong, mild, calm; wind direction (from); thunder/lightening etc.

suggested_learning_activities.description: Learners list all the elements used to describe the weather. Ask 'What is the difference between weather and climate?'
Learners visit a working weather station... make their own equipment, where practical, such as Okta grids for measuring cloud cover and rain gauges.
Learners work in groups, using their collected weather data to create charts and graphs that help to explain daily variations.
Explain and show examples of recording weather on maps by lines, symbols or shading e.g. temperature (isotherms), rainfall (isohyets), pressure (isobars).
Learners look for pictures of cloud types on the Internet.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe learners as they discuss and explain their weather data and how it influences everyday activity.
Observe learners’ use of appropriate terminology as they record data using instruments and report back.
Observe group dialogue as they prepare their presentation and their explanation of the work produced.

themes.theme_description: Location, Size, Relief, Formation of Landforms, Climate, Vegetation, Climate Change.

topic_metadata.topic_title: LOCATION, SIZE, AND RELIEF REGIONS OF EAST AFRICA

topics.core_competency: After studying this topic, the learner should be able to know the countries making up East Africa; their comparative sizes in area and population; and the main relief regions they can be divided into.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: use maps, statistics, graphs and diagrams to analyse population (s)
appreciate that East African countries vary greatly in area and population (a, gs)
know the East African countries, their approximate population and area (k)
use contours to show physical features on maps and draw cross-sections from simple contour maps (s)

syllabus_notes.text_verbatim: Explain that in this syllabus we are using the traditional idea of East Africa as Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania.

suggested_learning_activities.description: Learners answer questions about the countries making up East Africa to determine what they know about their comparative size and population. They then work in groups to research and create their own table of information regarding this.

Learners study one or more local features through fieldwork, collecting samples, taking photographs and creating a labelled map display to show the physical environment and the influence of relief on weather and climate.
Learners work in groups to draw a map showing relief regions and collaborate to identify and explain regions where there is or has been a high hazard risk.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe learners as they collect information and create their graphs and diagrams: ask them to describe what their maps show and how accurate they believe the information to be.
Observe learners as they describe and locate key landscape features through fieldwork and research on their map and add correctly labelled images.
Observe learners’ explanations of their map and judgement of hazardous areas.

topic_metadata.topic_title: FORMATION OF MAJOR LANDFORMS AND DRAINAGE IN EAST AFRICA

topics.core_competency: After studying this topic, the learner should be able to explain how each of the main types of landforms in East Africa was formed, the main types of rocks and the main features of the drainage.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: know the main types of landforms and drainage features of East Africa(k)
understand how igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks are formed, that they are made up of minerals, and that some minerals are useful (u)
understand the process of weathering and how weathered rock particles form the basis of soil (u)
understand how each of the main types of landform was formed: by rocks themselves or by the rocks being worn away or eroded away (u)
understand the characteristics of the main types of rocks and their effect on soils.(u)
understand the relationship between drainage the landforms. (u)
recognize the landforms on photographs. (s)
locate the examples of landforms on maps of East Africa. (s)
appreciate that the landforms, rocks and drainage all affect the way people live. (v/a, gs)
understand the main concepts of plate tectonics and how this has led to the formation of the main physical features of East Africa (u)
understand the characteristics of important kinds of physical features in East Africa, including mountain ranges, volcanoes, plateaus, basins and rift valleys (u)
study through field work any of the above physical features in the local area (s)
draw a map to show the main relief regions of East Africa (s)
recognise physical features from photographs (s)
understand how their own lives and the lives of their communities are affected by physical features, including natural hazards (u)
understand through case studies how the physical features affect the lives of people in selected areas of East Africa (u)
draw diagrams to show the formation of important physical features (s)

must_cover: Types of rock: Metamorphic, Volcanic/Igneous, Sedimentary
Formation of landforms: Plateaus, Mountains, Rift Valleys, Plains

suggested_learning_activities.description: produce a commentary about the formation of a particular type of landscape and its geology; write a case study on a type of landscape feature such as a river, volcano or lake and how it affects human and physical landscape
debate the merits of living near or on a particular feature, explaining the pros and cons.
Learners look for diagrams of faulting on Internet. Learners look for diagrams and pictures of volcanoes in east Africa on Internet.
Observe any steep slope outside the classroom. Ask: What happens to the soil when it rains? Observe a gentle area. What happens to some of the soil which is washed away?
Explain that a tiny creature called a coral polyp lives in some areas of sea near the shore.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe how well learners make links when explaining a landscape between the appearance, geology and the process involved.
Observe how effectively learners express their views about living near a particular type of feature e.g. a volcano?
Observe how well learners use correct terminology and locate features accurately on maps.

topic_metadata.topic_title: CLIMATE AND NATURAL VEGETATION OF EAST AFRICA

topics.core_competency: After studying this topic, the learner should be able to describe and explain the main types of climate in East Africa and how the climate influences the vegetation, appreciating this as a natural resource which can be used to benefit the present and future generations.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: understand the characteristics of the climates of Uganda and the rest of East Africa and the factors influencing them (u)
understand through fieldwork the characteristics of the vegetation and how vegetation is affected by the climates (u)
draw graphs to show the different climates (s)
draw a map showing the climates and vegetation of East Africa (s)
recognise and describe a climate from a graph (s)
recognise and describe types of vegetation from photographs. (s)
understand through case studies how selected climates and types of vegetation affect the way of life of the people in those areas (u)

must_cover: Factors affecting climates: Temperature, Rainfall, Height, Relief, Winds, Vegetation
Types of climate: Equatorial, Savannah, Semi-arid, Mountain, Coastal

suggested_learning_activities.description: In pairs, learners: select sources to answer given questions and use research to accurately complete a climate zone map of the region; add a key to show vegetation.
Show climate graph for each type of climate, un-named. Learners: describe climate from graph; answer questions and describe type of climate.
Learners draw sketch map to show climatic regions of East Africa.
Show photographs of each type of vegetation. Learners describe vegetation and suggest, with reasons, what type of climate it comes from.
Learners look for and describe photographs of each type of vegetation on the Internet.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Learners write their own questions and produce their paired maps. Observe these questions and maps and evaluate how well learners have been able to understand characteristics of vegetation and climate.
Learners take turns in each pair to answer questions from other members of the class; they explain how people in different climate zones might live and why.

topic_metadata.topic_title: CLIMATE CHANGE IN EAST AFRICA AND THE WORLD

topics.core_competency: After studying this topic, the learner should understand what is meant by climate change, what is causing it and its effects in East Africa.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: understand the concept of climate change and its indicators and be able to draw diagrams to show the causes of climate change (s)
understand the possible causes of climate change (u)
understand the political and other difficulties faced in addressing climate change and carrying out measures to reduce its effects (u)
understand how climate change may affect Uganda and the rest of East Africa (u)
understand possible ways in which local communities and government can reduce the effects of climate change (u)
use two case studies to examine the possible effects of climate change in other areas of Africa and the world (u)
form opinions about measures to reduce or mitigate climate change (a)
participate in tree planting and other activities which might alleviate the effects of climate change in their own communities/school (s)
appreciate the need for people and governments to take actions to help reduce climate change, and change their lives to mitigate or reduce the effects of climate change (a, gs)

suggested_learning_activities.description: Learners research the meaning of climate change using different sources and think critically about the definitions before reporting back with an explanation of their chosen one.
Students investigate how some degree of global warming makes this planet habitable... and the enhanced global warming process.
Learners work in groups, taking on the roles of government ministers with different views about the relative importance of people, the economy and the environment.
Ask learners to ask old people, especially farmers and people who fish, whether they have noticed any changes in the weather patterns or seasons in recent years.
Use diagram and questions to explain the effect of these gases in the atmosphere... Learners copy diagram.
Learners look up the Paris agreement or any other agreement on climate change on Internet and summarise main parts of agreement.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Learners should explain the distinction between climate change and human-induced climate change.
Learners draw a diagram to show what causes climate change and explain this in their own words, using appropriate vocabulary.
In conversation, ask learners to explain the difference between weather and climate.
In conversation, ask learners to suggest what could be done in their communities to help reduce the causes of climate change and to mitigate or reduce the effects of climate change.

themes.theme_title: World Climates: Introduction to North America; Agriculture in East Africa and North America
themes.theme_description: Major climatic zones, North America regions, Agriculture comparisons (Prairies, California).

topic_metadata.topic_title: MAJOR CLIMATIC ZONES OF THE WORLD

topics.core_competency: After studying this topic, the learner should be able to locate and describe the major climatic zones of the world and understand the relationship between climate and human activities and the lifestyles in each zone.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: know the names of some of the major climatic regions of the world (k)
understand the main characteristics of the climates and how each affects the vegetation of the area (u)
understand the factors influencing these characteristics (u)
understand how people’s ways of life are influenced by the climate in each region (u)
plot the major climatic regions on a world map (s)
recognise each type of region on photographs (s)
understand how the traditional farming and way of life was influenced by the climate (u)
appreciate that people’s lifestyles are influenced by the type of weather and climate (a)
appreciate that this influence is becoming less as technology helps people to overcome difficulties of their climate and as people move into urban areas. (a, gs)

must_cover: Factors affecting climates: latitude, distance from sea, height, relief, winds, vegetation
Major regions: Tropical (Equatorial, Savannah, Desert), Temperate (Coastal, Inland), Polar

suggested_learning_activities.description: In pairs, learners: choose any other area of Uganda with a different type of climate to that of your own locality; describe this type of climate; show the difference between the two types and the reasons for the differences.
Show these areas on a wall map or sketch map of the world on BB or look up types of climate on Internet. Show the following types of climate on a world map and learners summarise on a table.
Learners research the type of climate on the Internet, thinking about sources and comparing information.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Ask learners to describe the climate of their home area and explain how it is influenced by the different things they have learnt about in this topic.
In conversation, learners suggest one effect that each of the major climatic regions of the world might have on the way people live and are able to offer an explanation.
Ask learners to produce a table which outlines the types of climate.

topics.core_competency: After studying this topic, the learner should know the main physical features, drainage, and climates of North America and brief history of North America.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: know the countries of North America (k)
understand the main physical features of North America (s)
know the main climatic regions of North America (s)
understand how the size and position of North America makes it different from East Africa (s)
understand how and why North America has developed differently from East Africa (u)
draw a sketch map showing the countries and main regions of North America (s)
appreciate the usefulness of learning about areas outside East Africa or Africa to contrast with East Africa (a, gs)
appreciate that all areas of the world are different, depending on their position and history (a, gs)
describe some climatic regions of North America, using climate graphs and compare these to East Africa (s)

must_cover: Countries: USA, Canada, Mexico, West Indies
Physical features: Rocky Mountains, Great Plains, Appalachian Mountains, Mississippi/Missouri basin

explicitly_excluded.text_verbatim: note: main features only, not a detailed study of N. America

depth_limitations.text_verbatim: learners get general impression of North America, not detailed geography

suggested_learning_activities.description: In pairs, learners have a large blank outline of North America and a list of features you wish them to learn about. Give them a timed challenge to mark them on the map... then give the pairs a timed period to research atlases, globes and the Internet to create a new map with the features correctly located.
Ask learners if North America is bigger than Africa; has higher mountains; has bigger rivers; has bigger towns?

Working in groups, learners use drawn or digital maps or both, each group taking a climate zone of North America and using climate graphs, they describe, compare and contrast the climate overseas with that in Africa.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Learners speak about their own views and identify some influences from North America, especially USA, on East Africa, including their own lives?
Observe as learners compare North America with Africa, showing the main differences in terms of features and climate and explain why this is so.
Ask learners to produce a model or infographic to describe features of North America.

topic_metadata.topic_title: DEVELOPMENT OF AGRICULTURE IN EAST AFRICA

topics.core_competency: After studying this topic, the learner should know and understand the main differences between agriculture in North America and agriculture in East Africa and whether methods used in North America are appropriate for Uganda.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: carry out a field study to find out the nature of the land and water resources in the local area and the use of land and water resources for agriculture (s)
understand the main types of agriculture in Uganda and the rest of East Africa and the factors influencing them (u)
appreciate the importance of land and water as a source of food, livelihood and income for families, clans and communities (a)
Understand the differences between subsistence and commercial agriculture, and small scale and large- scale agriculture. (u)
understand the advantages and disadvantages of each of the main types of arable agriculture. (u)
know the characteristics of traditional pastoral farming. (k)
understand the advantages and disadvantages of commercial pastoral farming. (u)
form opinions about the dangers of over- use of land and water resources and the need to conserve these in the local area
recognise different types of farming from photographs (s)
draw diagrams to show seasonal activities on farms (s)
draw maps to show different types of farming (s)
appreciate the importance of agriculture in the economies of East Africa (a, gs)
appreciate the need for government policies which assist farmers and develop farming (a, gs)
appreciate that caring for and preserving resources in the local environment, community and country are signs of love for one’s country
understand possible ways in which local communities and governments can reduce the effects of climate change (u)
take part in activities to improve local land and water resources

suggested_learning_activities.description: If possible, learners visit a farming area, or think of any farming area they know, and report on the size of farms, type of farming, crops grown, and animals kept, methods used etc.

Learners collaborate in groups to research different kinds of farming and make judgements about the relative importance and appropriateness... Learners use maps, photographs, graphs and diagrams to support their presentation.
Tell learners to imagine that they have inherited a small area of land in their home area in Uganda. In conversation, ask them to suggest how they would farm it in order to provide a good income.
Whole-class discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of plantation farming.
Learners look up soil conservation on Internet and describe how it applies to East Africa.
Discuss the advantages and challenges of traditional pastoralists changing to partly commercial farming by sale of cattle and milk.
Using photographs and diagrams learners describe the methods of irrigation.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe learners as they describe any farm in East Africa, the methods used, problems encountered and suggest ways of improvement.

Ask learners to imagine that they were the Minister of Agriculture in an East African country. Observe how well they are able to write a policy or list of ideas about how to improve agriculture in that country.
In conversation, ask learners to suggest reasons why we should increase irrigation in Uganda and suggest the best methods to do this.

topic_metadata.topic_title: SOME AGRICULTURAL AREAS OF NORTH AMERICA: LARGE SCALE FARMING IN THE PRAIRIES; IRRIGATED FARMING IN CALIFORNIA

topics.core_competency: After studying this topic, the learner should know and understand the main differences between agriculture in North America and agriculture in East Africa and whether methods used in North America are appropriate for Uganda.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: know some important types of agriculture in North America; important crops grown and animals kept (k)
understand the main differences between agriculture in North America and East Africa and the reasons for these differences (u)
suggest whether some agricultural methods from North America are suitable for East Africa (v/a)
use a range of sources including maps, photographs, Internet tables and graphs to research relevant information (s)
locate the main types of agriculture on a map of North America (s)
appreciate why methods of agriculture used in North America are not always suitable for Uganda (a, gs)
appreciate that development of agriculture depends on the level of economic development and technology (v/a, gs)

suggested_learning_activities.description: In groups, learners brainstorm useful questions that will help them answer the big question about the difference between agriculture in North America and East Africa... learners use a mix of given and researched evidence to gain a general overview to investigate a particular region and write a case study report.
Use a table of the percentage of people in USA and Uganda working in agriculture, industries and services... Ask learners what this shows about the different methods of agriculture.
Learners work in pairs to study the photo(s) [of Prairie farm] and answer questions about relief, field size, crops, labour, etc.
Working in groups, learners discuss: could this method be used in most parts of East Africa? Why not? Would this be a good method for East Africa?
Put questions about California irrigated farming on OHP/BB and learners discuss in pairs (describe land, crops, water supply, labour).

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe learners as they describe the main differences between large scale extensive farming in the Prairies and irrigated farming in Central California; they explain whether some farming practices would be good for East Africa and give reasons.
Observe learners debate on the best way to improve agriculture in East Africa: by large scale mechanized farming or small-scale intensive farming?
